tiers: Foundation/Higher (one tier for all four papers)

assessment.title: Listening and understanding in Arabic
assessment.duration: Foundation 35 min; Higher 45 min (each includes 5 min reading time)
assessment.format: Multiple-response and short open-response. Foundation: Section A 12 questions in English, Section B two in Arabic. Higher: Section A two in Arabic, Section B eight in English. No dictionaries.

assessment.title: Speaking in Arabic
assessment.duration: Foundation 7 to 9 min; Higher 10 to 12 min; plus 12 min supervised preparation
assessment.content: All five themes; conversation uses two themes.
assessment.format: Role play (10 marks), picture-based task (24), conversation (36). Student chooses the first conversation topic two weeks ahead; Pearson sets the second theme. Internally conducted, externally assessed, April/May window.

assessment.title: Reading and understanding in Arabic
assessment.format: Ten questions in three sections: A in English, B in Arabic, C a translation from Arabic into English. Texts include advertisements, emails, letters, articles and literary texts.

assessment.title: Writing in Arabic
assessment.duration: Foundation 1 hour 20 min; Higher 1 hour 25 min
assessment.format: Foundation: three open-response questions and one translation into Arabic. Higher: two open-response questions and one translation into Arabic. Instructions in Arabic; vocalisation not expected.

nonExam: Speaking (Paper 2) is conducted in the centre by teachers, recorded and marked externally. No coursework.

examEntry.summary: Taught from the UK GCSE specification above; pupils are entered for Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Arabic (First Language) (4AA1).
examEntry.label: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4AA1
examEntry.papers: Paper 1 Reading, Summary and Grammar (4AA1/01): 2 hours 15 minutes, 75 marks, 60% (reading on two texts 49 marks, summary of a third text 6, grammar 20). Paper 2 Writing (4AA1/02): 1 hour 30 minutes, 50 marks, 40%, two 25-mark tasks from a choice of three.
examEntry.privateCandidates: Written papers only: no listening paper and no speaking test, so nothing has to be conducted by a teacher at the centre (unlike 1AA0 Paper 2).
notes: 4AA1 is a first-language qualification. We found no Pearson International GCSE in Arabic as a foreign language, so 4AA1 is the matching International GCSE.

It asks more than 1AA0 in reading and grammar: longer authentic texts, a summary task, and grammar questions that use grammatical terminology. Add explicit grammar teaching (with the Arabic terms), summary writing and extended writing to the 1AA0 course from Year 10.
1AA0 listening, speaking and translation are not examined in 4AA1. Keep them in lessons for language development, but weight Year 11 towards reading, grammar and writing.
The 4AA1 topics (youth, education, media, culture, sport and leisure, travel and tourism, work, environment, health, technology) overlap with the 1AA0 themes.
Confirm the entry for each pupil by the end of Year 10: a pupil far from first-language level may do better in 1AA0, if a centre will run its speaking test.
examEntry.regulation: International GCSEs are not regulated by Ofqual. Pearson describes them as generally equivalent to GCSEs; sixth forms and universities set their own entry rules.

links.topic: Vocabulary of worship, festivals and belief (Ramadan, Eid)
links.how: Arabic supplies the language for festivals; Islamic Studies explains their meaning.

links.topic: Reading Arabic script, vowels and sounds
links.how: Qur'an lessons secure letter shapes and pronunciation that carry over to Arabic reading and speaking.
English grammar terms (tense, agreement, plural) help pupils analyse Arabic; translation builds precision in both.
Geography supplies place and climate content that pupils describe in Arabic.
Pupils discuss green living and resources in Arabic, drawing on Geography knowledge.

links.topic: Healthy eating, technology and social media, friendship
links.how: PSHE gives the issues; Arabic gives the vocabulary for opinions and advantages and disadvantages.
Careers content is the context for describing ambitions and professions in Arabic.
Cultural context for the spec's requirement to study topics in Arabic-speaking communities.
Listening to Arabic songs and drama builds listening skills and cultural knowledge.

gaps: Assessment objective codes and weightings were not read (the spec contents page places them near page 62).
Grammar list (Appendix 2) and vocabulary list (Appendix 3) were not read. The spec says the vocabulary lists are a non-exhaustive guide; no word count was seen.

Whether the qualification is still current for teaching in 2026-27 is unconfirmed. The pages opened give no end or withdrawal date, and Pearson exam materials dated August 2025 appeared in search results. Check with Pearson.
Papers 1 to 4 detail for the Higher tier was read from the specification only; sample assessment materials were read only for Foundation Papers 1 and 2.
The school's Drive holds a Pearson 2017 GCSE Arabic scheme of work. It was not opened for this file.
Year placement follows the school's Year 10 lesson content (Theme 1 in Y10) and is otherwise a recommended sequence; the school has no Year 11 Arabic lesson file yet.
Command-word taxonomy, mark grids for Paper 4 and the dialect policy were not recorded. The spec refers only to standard Arabic.
